There can be a lot of value in wind and solar power that isnt easily calculated up to make a direct comparison to traditional power plants, or to give simple explanations for conversations like this. Things to think about are demand patterns (demand peaks during the day and there's little demand overnight), transmission loss (the further power has to travel through the lines, the more of it is lost by the time it reaches its destination) and operational costs versus fixed upfront costs to build something. There is added cost to build the infrastructure to transmit power, and infrastructure to transport fuel to a power plant. Is the power predictable and on-demand or is it out of our control?

Solar, wind, coal, nuclear, natural gas, and hydroelectric all have different cost profiles and there is value in having different types to compensate for the weaknesses of the others. It's beneficial to have diverse sources of power to hedge against spikes in fuel price.

Urban areas will typically have coal plants, but coal plants cant turn off so they produce excess power at night. They have natural gas plants to run during peak hours and shut off at night. In more rural areas these plants might be very far away and transmission loss makes wind power more cost competitive if it can be built closer to the consumers. Flat areas like the great plains also tend to have higher wind speeds that make them well suited to wind turbines.

Power generation is big business and can have a big impact on local economies, there are a lot of really smart people working on that stuff. Utility companies are publicly regulated and rate hikes have to be approved by utility boards. In all but the most leftist dominated states and local areas, it's a safe bet that if there are wind turbines somewhere there is a sound economic reason for them being there.
